questions.q: The Armstrong axiom of augmentation says that:
options: If Y is a subset of X then X → Y
If X → Y and Y → Z then X → Z
If X → YZ then X → Y and X → Z
If X → Y then XZ → YZ for any set of attributes Z
questions.explanation: Augmentation says that adding the same attributes Z to both sides of a dependency keeps it true.

questions.q: Which of the following rules is derived from Armstrong's axioms and is NOT one of the three basic axioms?
questions.explanation: The three basic axioms are reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity. Union, decomposition and pseudotransitivity can be proved from them.

questions.q: In R(A, B, C, D, E) the functional dependencies are A → B, B → C and C → D. What is the closure A⁺?
questions.explanation: Start with {A}. A → B adds B, B → C adds C, and C → D adds D. Nothing determines E, so A⁺ = {A, B, C, D}.

questions.q: R(A, B, C, D, E) has the dependencies AB → C, C → D and D → E. What is the candidate key of R?
questions.explanation: A and B appear on no right-hand side, so both must be in every key. AB⁺ = {A, B, C, D, E}, so AB is a key, and it is minimal because A⁺ = {A} and B⁺ = {B}.

questions.q: R(A, B, C) has the dependencies A → B, B → C and C → A. How many candidate keys does R have?
questions.explanation: A⁺, B⁺ and C⁺ are each {A, B, C}, so A, B and C are all candidate keys. That gives 3 candidate keys.

questions.q: A relation is in First Normal Form (1NF) when:
options: All attribute values are atomic (no repeating groups or multivalued attributes)
Every determinant is a candidate key
questions.explanation: 1NF only demands atomic values in every column. The other options describe 2NF, 3NF and BCNF.

questions.q: A relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and:
options: It has no partial dependency of a non-prime attribute on a part of a candidate key
It has only one candidate key
questions.explanation: 2NF removes partial dependencies: a non-prime attribute must depend on the whole candidate key, not on just a part of it.

questions.q: A relation is in 3NF if it is in 2NF and:
options: It has no transitive dependency of a non-prime attribute on the key
questions.explanation: 3NF removes transitive dependencies such as Key → A and A → B, where B is a non-prime attribute.

questions.q: A relation is in BCNF if, for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y:
questions.explanation: BCNF is stricter than 3NF: the left side of every non-trivial dependency must be a super key.

questions.q: R(StudentID, CourseID, StudentName) has the candidate key (StudentID, CourseID) and the dependency StudentID → StudentName. What is the highest normal form of R?
questions.explanation: StudentName depends on only a part of the key (StudentID), which is a partial dependency. So 2NF is violated and R is only in 1NF.

questions.q: R(A, B, C) has the dependencies A → B and B → C. The candidate key is A. What is the highest normal form of R?
questions.explanation: The key is a single attribute, so no partial dependency exists and R is in 2NF. But A → B → C is a transitive dependency of C on the key, so R is not in 3NF.

questions.q: R(A, B, C) has the dependencies AB → C and C → B. What is the highest normal form of R?
questions.explanation: The candidate keys are AB and AC, so A, B and C are all prime attributes. C → B is allowed in 3NF because B is prime, but C is not a super key, so BCNF is violated.

questions.q: Every relation that has only two attributes is in:
questions.explanation: With two attributes, any non-trivial dependency has the other attribute on its right side, so its left side is a key. Hence every binary relation is in BCNF.

questions.q: Which statement is always true?
questions.explanation: The normal forms are nested: BCNF ⊂ 3NF ⊂ 2NF ⊂ 1NF. A relation in 3NF may still fail BCNF, as the example AB → C, C → B shows.

questions.q: An update anomaly occurs when:
options: The same fact is stored in many rows, so changing it in only some rows leaves the data inconsistent
A new row cannot be inserted without inserting unrelated data
Deleting a row also loses unrelated facts
A table has no primary key
questions.explanation: Redundancy causes update anomalies. The second option describes an insertion anomaly and the third a deletion anomaly. Normalization removes all three.

questions.q: Cost-based query optimization chooses an evaluation plan using:
options: Only the order in which the tables are written in the query
Statistics such as the number of tuples, blocks and distinct values to estimate the cost of each plan
questions.explanation: A cost-based optimizer estimates the cost of several equivalent plans using statistics from the catalog and picks the cheapest one.

questions.q: R(A, B, C) with F = {A → B} is decomposed into R1(A, B) and R2(A, C). This decomposition is:
questions.explanation: The common attribute A is a key of R1 (A → B), so joining R1 and R2 gives back R exactly (lossless). A → B lies completely inside R1, so it is preserved.

questions.q: A decomposition is dependency preserving if:
options: It has fewer tables than the original
Every decomposed table has a primary key
The natural join of the tables gives back the original relation
All functional dependencies of the original relation can be checked on the decomposed tables without joining them
questions.explanation: Dependency preservation is about enforcing the dependencies without joins. The third option describes a lossless-join decomposition, which is a different property.

questions.q: Which statement about decomposition is correct?
options: A lossless and dependency preserving decomposition into 3NF is always possible
A lossless and dependency preserving decomposition into BCNF is always possible
A decomposition into 3NF can never be lossless
questions.explanation: 3NF always allows a decomposition that is both lossless and dependency preserving. BCNF is always lossless, but may lose some dependencies.

questions.q: Which decomposition of R(A, B, C) with F = {A → B} is lossy?
options: R1(A, B) and R2(A, B, C)
R1(A, C) and R2(A, B, C)
questions.explanation: For {AB, BC} the common attribute B determines neither A nor C, so joining can create spurious tuples. In the other options the common attributes form a key of one part.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the steps in query processing?
questions.explanation: The query is first parsed and translated into relational algebra, then the optimizer picks the best plan, and finally the evaluation engine executes it.

questions.q: Which of the following equivalence rules is correct?
options: Join is not commutative, so R ⋈ S and S ⋈ R can give different tuples
A selection with two conditions can never be split into two selections
Join is associative only when all tables have the same size
questions.explanation: Selections can be applied in any order with the same result. Natural join is commutative and associative, which lets the optimizer reorder joins to reduce cost.

questions.q: In heuristic query optimization, which rule is applied first because it reduces the size of the intermediate results the most?
options: Perform selections as early as possible, before the joins
Perform all joins first and the selections at the end
questions.explanation: Applying selections (and projections) early removes unwanted tuples, so the joins that follow work on much smaller relations.

questions.q: A block nested-loop join of R (100 blocks, outer) and S (50 blocks, inner), with only one buffer block for each relation, needs how many block transfers in the worst case?
questions.explanation: The worst case is br × bs + br = 100 × 50 + 100 = 5,100 block transfers: every block of R is read once and S is scanned once for each block of R.

questions.q: Which join algorithm needs both relations to be sorted on the join attribute?
questions.explanation: Merge join scans both sorted relations once, moving through them in step. If the inputs are not sorted, they are sorted first, which is why it is also called sort-merge join.
